carnival: Under federal admiralty law, the unnegotiated cruise-ticket forum clause could bind the passengers if reasonable and fundamentally fair. Lack of bargaining alone did not defeat it; the Court did not approve every ticket term or every forum clause.
lucy: What counts is how your words and actions would look to a reasonable person, not what you secretly meant. If you act like you are making a serious deal, you are, even if you thought it was a joke.
specht: Clicking a button only agrees to terms you were fairly warned about. If the terms sit below the visible screen and nothing tells you the click means agreement, you have not agreed.
drennan: California protected the general contractor’s reasonable, foreseeable reliance on the subcontractor’s bid. Using the bid did not yet form a subcontract, but made the offer irrevocable long enough for a reasonable opportunity to accept after the main contract was awarded.
hawkins: If a doctor truly guarantees a result, breaking that guarantee is a contract claim. Damages are the gap between the hand you were promised and the hand you got, not the pain that any such operation would have involved.
bayliner: Precise numbers only create a warranty if they describe the thing you actually bought. Figures for a differently equipped boat and general sales praise do not promise how your boat will perform.
sullivan: A patient can sue on a surgeon's clear promise of a specific result even when the surgery was done without negligence. The recovery can cover the money spent, the worsening of the condition and the extra pain and distress the broken promise caused.
naval-institute: Contract damages make up the injured party's own loss. The breaching publisher's profits can be evidence of that loss, but profits that do not match what the plaintiff lost are not simply handed over.
morris-sparrow: Usually a disappointed buyer of goods gets money, not the goods. But when the item is one of a kind to the buyer, like a horse he personally trained, a court can order it delivered because money would not replace it.
white-benkowski: Even a deliberate, spiteful breach of contract does not bring punitive damages unless a separate tort is proved. A small award is still real compensation when the loss, like interrupted household water, is real but hard to price.
hamer: Giving up something you had a legal right to do, because someone promised to pay you for it, is enough to make the promise enforceable. It does not matter whether the promisor gained anything and that quitting was good for you.
dyer: Dropping a legal claim can be a real price for a promise even if the claim turns out to be worthless, so long as it was genuinely doubtful or you honestly believed it might win. Settlements made in good faith are protected.
tolosa: In Texas, a bank's promise to delay foreclosure on a large loan has to be in a signed writing. Saying you relied on an oral promise does not get around that unless the bank also promised to sign the paperwork.
mattei: A promise that depends on the promisor being satisfied is not an empty promise, because the law requires satisfaction to be judged honestly and in good faith. That duty is enough to make the deal binding on both sides.
structural-polymer: A promise to buy all you need from one seller is a real commitment even if you currently need nothing, because the Code requires you to order your actual needs in good faith. That obligation is the price that holds the contract together.
wood-lucy: A contract can contain a promise nobody wrote down. Reading the whole exclusive-agency deal in its business setting, Cardozo found an implied promise to use reasonable efforts, and that implied promise made the arrangement a real bargain.
ricketts: A grandfather's gift promise had no price attached, so it was not a bargain. But because he meant his granddaughter to quit her job in reliance on it and she did, his estate could not take the promise back for want of consideration.
feinberg: A company's promise of a pension was not paid for by past work or by any promise to keep working. It bound the company anyway, because the employee retired in reliance on it, just as the company should have expected.
cohen-cowles: A source who was promised confidentiality and then named in print can sue the newspaper for breaking that promise under promissory estoppel. A general law that applies to everyone does not become unconstitutional because a newspaper is the one who broke the promise.
dg-stout: A promise to keep an at-will relationship going cannot earn you the future profits you hoped for, because it could end at any time. It can still make the promisor pay for a real opportunity you gave up in reliance on it.
balfour: Everyday arrangements between a husband and wife living together, like a promised allowance, are not contracts. Courts presume the couple did not intend legal consequences unless the party suing proves otherwise.
lefkowitz: An advertisement becomes a binding offer when it is definite enough that nothing is left to negotiate: this item, this price, first come first served. Once a customer meets those terms, the store cannot add new conditions.
wucherpfennig: For this land-sale offer, acceptance had to communicate a definite, unconditional commitment to the offered terms. A response expressing readiness to proceed while requesting more information did not do that, so the seller could revoke. Goods transactions may follow different UCC formation rules.
international-filter: An offeror can decide how its offer is accepted. If it says approval by a company officer is enough, that approval completes the contract without any separate notice to the other side.
white-corlies: Deciding privately to accept an offer, and buying materials you could use for any job, does not tell the other party anything. Acceptance between people who are apart has to be an outward act sent their way.
dorton: Boilerplate on a seller's acknowledgment form does not block a contract just because it says the sale is subject to the seller's terms. Only language that clearly says the seller will not go forward without your agreement to those terms counts as expressly conditional.
citoh: When a seller's form says the deal is conditional on its extra terms, the buyer never agrees, and both sides perform anyway, the contract is made by their conduct. Its terms are only what both forms share, plus the Code's default rules; the seller's extra terms drop out.
bayway: Between merchants, UCC § 2-207 has three exceptions to including extra terms: the offer limits acceptance, the term materially alters the deal, or timely objection occurs. Bayway concerns material alteration: the opponent bears that burden, and personal surprise did not suffice against unrebutted industry practice.
northrop: The Seventh Circuit predicted that Illinois would use the knockout rule: conflicting terms in an offer and a nonconditional acceptance cancel out, and Code defaults fill the gap. It applied that approach to the competing warranty terms; this was a prediction of state law.
hill-gateway: The Seventh Circuit treated the boxed terms as an offer inviting acceptance by keeping the computer beyond the thirty-day return period, after a chance to read them. The buyers thereby accepted arbitration. Klocek illustrates a different formation analysis, so Hill is not a uniform rule for every boxed term.
klocek: The opposite answer to Hill v. Gateway. This court treated the buyer as the one making the offer, so terms arriving in the box were proposals to add terms, and a consumer who merely keeps the computer has not expressly agreed to them.
dixon: The complaint alleged that the bank told the borrowers to stop paying while it considered modification, then foreclosed. The district court predicted that Massachusetts law allowed this reliance claim to proceed despite indefinite modification terms. It denied dismissal; liability and damages still had to be proved.
cyberchron: No final contract was ever signed, but a clear promise that led a supplier to keep building in reliance can still be enforced. The remedy is the money spent in reliance, including properly attributed overhead, not the profits of the deal that never happened.
channel-home: The Third Circuit predicted that Pennsylvania would enforce a sufficiently definite, supported promise to negotiate in good faith, separate from the unfinished lease. It sent the case to trial to determine actual intent to be bound and the alleged time limit; it did not enforce a completed lease.
sun-printing: In this 1923 common-law decision, leaving both price and the period for that price to future agreement made the remaining arrangement unenforceable. A ceiling alone did not supply the missing duration. Modern goods-contract formation has a separate UCC route for some open terms.
oglebay: When the parties clearly meant a long-term deal to continue and their agreed price formulas stop working, a court can set a reasonable price itself and can order the parties to keep performing and keep negotiating.
alaska-packers: Applying the traditional pre-existing-duty rule to a services contract, the court refused to enforce the fishermen’s promised raise because they offered only work already owed. It did not hold that every requested increase was duress. Later modification exceptions and the UCC’s separate goods rule require their own analysis.
watkins: The parties to a contract can tear up the old price and agree a fairer new one in a single conversation. An owner who voluntarily agreed to pay more when the digging hit rock was held to the new rate.
austin: A modification extracted by threatening to cut off deliveries the supplier already owed is voidable for economic duress, but only if the victim could not get the goods elsewhere in time and a lawsuit for breach would not have been good enough.
swinton: Under the Massachusetts rule applied in 1942, the seller’s bare silence about termites did not support the pleaded tort claim without a misleading statement, concealment or duty to speak. Other jurisdictions and later disclosure statutes may impose duties; this is not a universal current rule for home sales.
kannavos: A seller who speaks must disclose the material facts needed to keep that statement from misleading the buyer. Advertising rental income while hiding the apartments’ illegal status created a deceptive impression and supported rescission. This duty concerns the subject discussed, rather than everything the seller knows.
speakers-sport: Telling an athlete you will get him millions in endorsements is sales talk, not a promise, when third parties decide whether to sign him. Competing for a client who can leave at any time is allowed unless you use fraud or other unlawful means.
vokes: The alleged expert flattery could support a fraud claim: instructors supposedly praised progress they knew was absent, while the student could not evaluate it equally. The Florida court let the complaint proceed; it did not decide that those allegations were proved.
masterson: A written deed does not automatically shut out an oral side agreement. If the side term is one the parties might naturally have left out of the writing and it does not contradict it, evidence of the term can come in.
bollinger: If both sides agreed to a term and it was left out of the writing by mistake, a court can rewrite the document to match the real deal. One party later denying the term does not prevent that when its own conduct proves the mistake.
pacific-gas: Under California’s approach, apparently clear words do not end the inquiry. A court provisionally considers outside evidence and admits it if relevant to a meaning the language can reasonably bear. The court reversed the exclusion here without deciding what coverage the parties actually intended.
www-associates: New York's answer to Pacific Gas: a complete and clear written contract means what it says, and a party cannot use outside evidence to manufacture an ambiguity or add terms the writing does not contain.
greenfield: A contract that transfers ownership of recordings without limit covers new uses the parties never mentioned. Silence about a particular use does not create an ambiguity, so the artists could not read in a reserved right.
trident: Even when the documents seem to leave no room for a borrower's reading, California law requires the court to at least hear the borrower's outside evidence of what the parties meant before ruling it out.
frigaliment: When a word like chicken has two trade meanings, the party claiming the narrower one has to prove it. Newcomers to a trade are bound by its usage only if they knew it or it was so settled they should have.
hurst: Numbers that look exact can carry a special trade meaning. Evidence that horse-meat traders treat 49.5 percent protein as meeting a 50 percent minimum could be used to read the written contract, even though it seemed unambiguous.
nanakuli: Under the Code, trade practice and the parties' own past performance are part of the contract. A posted-price term could be qualified by the paving trade's practice of price protection, with no need to first find the writing ambiguous.
columbia-nitrogen: Evidence of trade usage and past dealings comes in to explain a written sales contract unless it flatly cannot be squared with the express terms. The old rule that the writing first had to be ambiguous is gone under the Code.
dalton: A party that promises to use its discretion has to actually use it, and not arbitrarily. The testing service had to genuinely consider the student's evidence, though it did not have to prove he cheated, and the court ordered a real review rather than releasing the score.
northwest-ginsberg: Federal airline law preempted this Minnesota good-faith claim because it concerned prices and services and imposed duties beyond the airline’s voluntary promises. The Court did not reject every airline contract claim or every good-faith claim; the statutory connection and source of the duty matter.
market-street: Good faith in performing a contract does not require you to look after the other side's interests, but it forbids deliberately taking advantage of a mistake they are making about their own contract rights.
bloor: Best efforts did not require bankruptcy or substantial losses merely to promote this brand, but pursuing overall profit did not excuse ignoring the promised sales volume. Falstaff breached its brand-specific duty. Ordinary effort and expense cannot be dismissed merely because they reduce profit.
graham: A take-it-or-leave-it contract is still enforceable, but its terms must fit the weaker party's reasonable expectations and not be oppressive. An arbitration clause that let the other side's own union judge the dispute failed that test.
klar: Handing someone a claim check does not prove they agreed to the fine print on it. A parcel room that wants to limit its liability has to show the customer was reasonably told about the limit and accepted it.
doe-great-expectations: Applying New York’s 2005 dating-service statute, the court found Great Expectations’s forms unlawful and awarded recovery for those contracts. The decision concerned the then-applicable price, duration and referral requirements. Current § 394-c includes specific online-service exceptions, so the 2005 case does not supply the entire current regime.
williams-walker-thomas: A court can refuse to enforce a contract that was unconscionable when it was made: one side had no real choice and the terms were grossly one-sided. The court set out the test and sent the case back, without itself striking the contracts down.
stoll: A hidden clause that forced land buyers who could not read English to supply chicken litter worth far more than the land price was unconscionable. No meaningful choice plus shockingly one-sided terms means the clause will not be enforced.
blossom-farm: A seller normally gets paid even if the buyer plans to misuse the goods, but not when the seller actively helps the misuse. A supplier that knowingly furthered the cheese maker's improper use of its product could not collect the price.
xlo: For this New York antitrust defense, a facially lawful contract was not automatically unenforceable because of an alleged bid-rigging conspiracy. The issue was whether judgment would enforce the prohibited conduct itself. Factual questions remained, so the court refused dismissal rather than awarding the unpaid price.
hassler: In 2022, the Wyoming Supreme Court refused to rewrite an unreasonably broad noncompete to save it. That decision is historical guidance on judicial redrafting. Wyoming’s 2025 statute separately governs noncompetes entered on or after July 1, 2025, with a ban and specified exceptions.
luttinger: When a purchase depends on getting a mortgage on stated terms and the only available loan has a higher rate, the condition has failed and the buyers get their deposit back. The seller offering to make up the difference does not change that.
peacock: The Florida court read these ambiguous owner-payment clauses as setting a reasonable payment time, rather than shifting the owner’s nonpayment risk to the subcontractor. Transferring that risk required unambiguous language. The result depends on the clause and governing law; not every “pay after payment” clause has the same effect.
gibson: If you agree to paint a portrait that the customer may reject unless it satisfies him, his honest dissatisfaction ends the matter. It does not help that other people think the portrait is good.
kingston: Whether one party must perform before the other depends on the sense of the deal, not the order of the clauses. Because providing security was plainly meant to come before handing over the business, the buyer could not sue without first providing it.
jacob-youngs: A builder who innocently used a different brand of equally good pipe did not forfeit payment for the house. Trivial departures are compensated in damages, measured by the drop in value when tearing out the work would cost far more than it is worth.
gill: When a contract prices each item separately, a party can be paid for each item it fully delivered even though it did not finish the whole job. It gets nothing for items only partly carried out.
nelson-hazel: A contractor whose work fell short of substantial performance still cannot be made to hand over the value of the work for free. He recovers whatever the benefit to the owner exceeds the owner's damages.
mckenna: The owner repeatedly paid without demanding the architect’s certificate, then tried to use its absence as a complete defense to the final payment. On these facts, that conduct prevented forfeiture for honestly and substantially performed work. It does not mean that every ignored condition is permanently waived.
stees: The 1874 court held that latent soil problems did not excuse the builders’ unconditional promise: the building remained possible with suitable foundations or drainage. This historical strict-performance rule is part of the background to later impossibility, impracticability and risk-allocation doctrines.
renner: The shared mistake about water for a jojoba farm allowed rescission. Restitution covered the down payment and the value added to the returned land, minus its rental value; it did not reimburse all development spending. The amounts still had to be determined on remand.
taylor-caldwell: The parties’ bargain depended on this music hall’s continued existence, which the owners had not guaranteed. Its faultless destruction excused the promised concert performance, and the promoters could not recover their preparation losses. An express allocation of the destruction risk could produce a different result.
transatlantic: Closing Suez made the planned voyage more expensive, but sailing around Africa remained commercially practicable on this record. The shipper could not shift the extra cost to its customer. Impracticability examines the contingency, allocation of risk and severity of the burden; expense alone did not suffice here.
krell: The cancelled coronation procession defeated the shared foundation of this room-rental agreement: both parties understood that viewing it was the rental’s purpose. The court excused the unpaid balance. A disappointed personal motive alone is different; the event must be fundamental to the bargain and its risk must not have been allocated otherwise.
walgreen: A court may enforce a shopping-centre exclusivity clause with an injunction rather than damages when damages would be hard to measure. The choice turns on weighing the costs and benefits of each remedy in the particular case.
plante: A builder who substantially completed a house gets the price minus the cost of fixing defects. For a misplaced wall that did not change the home's value, the measure is the lost value, because tearing it out would be economic waste.
groves: The Minnesota court selected completion cost for the contractor’s deliberate failure to level the land, despite the smaller increase in land value. It remanded to determine the promised work and award. This contrasts with Peevyhouse’s Oklahoma approach; deliberate breach does not establish one national damages rule.
peevyhouse: The opposite outcome to Groves: a coal company that skipped the promised restoration of a farm paid only the small drop in the land's value, not the large cost of the work, because restoration was incidental to the lease's main purpose.
algernon-blair: A subcontractor driven off the job by the other side's serious breach can ask for the value of the work it did instead of contract damages. That value is not capped by the contract price, even if finishing the job would have lost money.
rockingham: Once a county told the bridge builder to stop, the builder could not keep building and bill for it. After a clear repudiation you recover what you had spent plus your expected profit, not costs you could have avoided.
parker: The studio could not reduce the actress’s recovery by pointing to a substitute role that was different and inferior. The employer had to prove reasonably available comparable employment; she did not have to accept that particular substitute. The court upheld her guaranteed-pay award.
hadley: Recoverable losses arise naturally from breach or were reasonably contemplated at formation as its probable result, including communicated special circumstances. The court treated the carrier as unaware that the mill would remain idle without this shaft, so it excluded those lost profits and ordered a new trial.
kenford: Unusual losses, like the rise in value of land around a stadium that was never built, are recoverable only if the breaching party could be seen to have taken on that risk when it made the contract. Foreseeing a loss is not the same as agreeing to pay for it.
fera: A new business is not automatically barred from recovering the profits it never got to earn. It needs a reasonable basis for estimating the loss, not mathematical certainty, and the jury may not simply guess.
figgie: Trade custom can make a limited remedy, such as repair, replace or refund, part of a sales contract even where it is unclear that the written terms were ever delivered. The remedy did not fail of its purpose when the refund alternative was actually carried out.
dave-gustafson: A per-day charge for finishing a highway late was enforceable because delay damages were genuinely hard to measure and the graduated amounts were a fair estimate. Actual loss became irrelevant once the clause was valid.
lake-river: A clause that guaranteed the bagging company its full revenue without deducting the costs it saved by not working was a penalty, not a reasonable estimate of damages, so Illinois law would not enforce it.
wassermans: A stipulated damages clause between commercial parties of equal strength is presumed reasonable and the challenger must prove otherwise. But a clause keyed to gross receipts can still be a penalty, and the court sent that question back for findings.
lawrence-fox: This landmark New York decision allowed the intended creditor beneficiary to enforce a promise supported by consideration from the debtor, although the beneficiary paid nothing. Six judges affirmed, but they did not share one rationale. It illustrates an early beneficiary-enforcement route, rather than the origin of all third-party-beneficiary law.
seaver: A niece could enforce her uncle's promise to his dying wife to leave the niece money. A promise made for a close family member's direct benefit is enforceable by her even though no one owed her a debt.
sisney-state: An inmate could not sue on the prison's food-service contract because the contract was made for the State's benefit and any benefit to inmates was incidental. Government contracts are presumed not to give private people enforceable rights.
sisney-reisch: The South Dakota court allowed Sisney’s contract claim to survive dismissal: the State’s agreement could waive immunity for its contractual obligations, and he plausibly alleged an intended benefit for inmates. That did not prove breach or establish that every government contract waives immunity.
psenicska: Applying New York law, the court held that the releases specifically disclaimed reliance on the subject of the alleged Borat deception, defeating the necessary reasonable reliance. The peculiar-knowledge exception did not apply on this record. A disclaimer’s wording and applicable exceptions matter; the court did not find that no misrepresentation occurred.
gianni: When a writing completely covers its subject, an earlier oral promise on that subject ordinarily cannot add a term that would naturally have appeared in the writing. Pennsylvania treated this lease as complete on the disputed sales rights, so Gianni’s claimed oral exclusivity promise was excluded.
teevee-toons: Under the international sales convention there is no parol evidence rule, so a merger clause excludes earlier oral understandings only if both parties actually meant it to. Evidence of the negotiations had to be considered.
ng-giap: Singapore's court implies a term only when necessary to make the contract work, and declined to imply a general duty of good faith into every contract. An entire-agreement clause shuts out implied terms only if it says so clearly.
anderson-binance: The district court rejected arbitration of the remaining pre-amendment claims: posting alone had not supplied adequate notice, and the amendment did not reach accrued claims. All five plaintiffs later acquired actual notice through the litigation. The decision did not resolve the later claims they had dismissed.
klein-pepsico: A buyer of a corporate jet could not force the sale through just because replacement planes cost more. Specific performance of a sale of goods needs a unique item or other proper circumstances, and adequate money damages rule it out.
cosby: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court held that this prosecutor’s unconditional decision intentionally induced Cosby’s reasonable, detrimental surrender of Fifth Amendment protection in civil depositions. Due process required enforcement on that record. Four Justices barred prosecution on these particular charges; the decision does not enforce every prosecutorial assurance.
shoe: A company does not need an office in a state to be sued there. If it sends salesmen into the state year after year and the lawsuit grows out of that business, it has enough ties that being sued there is fair. Courts look at what the company actually did, not at where it is said to be present.
wwvw: A state cannot reach a seller just because a customer drove the product there. The New York car dealer and distributor sold only in the Northeast, and the buyers themselves brought the Audi to Oklahoma. The seller must have done something to link itself to the state.
burger: A defendant can face a lawsuit arising from a deliberate, substantial business relationship with a company in another state, even without going there. In this case, the franchisee’s twenty-year relationship with Miami headquarters supported Florida jurisdiction, and he did not show that litigating there was unreasonable.
ford: Ford extensively advertised, sold and serviced the same models in the states where resident plaintiffs were injured. That supported jurisdiction even though the particular cars were first sold elsewhere. “Relate to” permits this close connection without requiring the in-state business to have caused the injury.
cp-capron: A plaintiff who picked a federal court can still win a reversal by pointing out that the record never showed the court had the power to hear the case. Choosing the forum does not stop you from later attacking its authority.
cp-tickle: Fraud by a party or its agent that induces an otherwise unreachable nonresident to enter the state can invalidate personal service there. The West Virginia court held the challenge legally sufficient if the inducement was proved; it did not itself establish fraud or finally quash service.
cp-pennoyer: Pennoyer’s 1878 territorial framework invalidated this personal judgment and the later land sale: Neff was absent, had not appeared, and the land had not first been brought under court control. International Shoe and Shaffer later changed the jurisdictional analysis; in-state service is not the only modern basis for suing a nonresident.
cp-hess: A state can say that driving on its roads counts as agreeing to be served through a state official. So a nonresident driver who causes a crash can be sued there. The law was fair because the driver was told about the suit and had time to defend.
cp-mcgee: One insurance policy sold into a state can be enough to let that state's courts hear a suit over that policy. The insurer's only California tie was a single policy sold by mail, but the suit was about that very policy, so California could hear it.
cp-hanson: A state cannot claim power over a company just because someone else moved there. The trust was set up in Delaware, and the settlor later moving to Florida was her own choice. The trustee had done nothing to reach into Florida, so Florida courts had no hold on it.
cp-gray: The Illinois Supreme Court in 1961 allowed suit over a valve that entered ordinary distribution and injured someone in Illinois, where its use was contemplated. That was Illinois’s stream-of-commerce approach; later Supreme Court decisions divided over what additional forum-directed conduct, if any, is necessary.
cp-keeton: A magazine that sells thousands of copies in a state every month can be sued there for libel, and the whole nationwide harm can be argued in that one suit. The plaintiff's own lack of ties to the state does not matter. What counts is what the publisher did there.
cp-calder: California was the focal point of both the allegedly libelous story and its harm. The reporter and editor’s own intentional conduct was expressly aimed there, supporting jurisdiction over them individually. Knowing that a plaintiff lives in a state and will feel harm there, by itself, is insufficient.
cp-kulko: Letting your child live with the other parent in another state is not a choice to enjoy that state's protection. A father who agreed that his children would live in California with their mother could not be pulled into a California court over child support.
cp-asahi: Even when a company has some tie to a state, a court can refuse to hear the case if it would be too unfair. A Japanese valve maker was being asked to defend a leftover indemnity claim in California, which was too burdensome. The justices split on what counts as enough contact.
cp-nicastro: A foreign manufacturer that sells through a distributor and aims at the whole United States is not automatically open to suit in every state. One machine reaching New Jersey was not enough. No single reasoning won five votes, and the Court did not say which view controls.
cp-walden: Your claim against a defendant is not enough just because you live in the state and felt the harm there. The defendant must have made a real connection with the state itself. An officer who seized cash in Georgia was not reachable in Nevada merely because the travelers lived there.
cp-goodyear: Indirect tire sales did not make the foreign subsidiaries essentially at home in North Carolina, so they could not face this unrelated accident claim there. Contacts-based general jurisdiction usually belongs at incorporation or the principal place of business. Consent is a separate basis, addressed later in Mallory.
cp-perkins: A company that has moved its real business operations into a state can be sued there even for claims unrelated to that business. The mining company ran its wartime business from Ohio, so Ohio could hear a stock claim. The Constitution allows it but does not force the state to.
cp-helicopteros: Buying equipment and sending staff for training in a state does not make a foreign company at home there. A Colombian helicopter operator that bought helicopters and trained pilots in Texas could not be sued in Texas over a crash in Peru unrelated to those trips.
cp-daimler: Being big and doing lots of business in a state does not make a company at home there. A German carmaker could not be sued in California over events in Argentina just because its American subsidiary sold cars across California.
cp-bnsf: BNSF’s substantial Montana operations did not make it at home there, and these workers’ injuries had no Montana connection. FELA’s provision addressed venue and subject-matter jurisdiction, not personal jurisdiction. The Court rejected these asserted grounds while leaving the workers’ separate consent argument undecided.
cp-bristol-myers: People hurt in other states cannot join a state's lawsuit just because the drugmaker does a lot of business there. Each claim needs its own tie to the state. Out-of-state plaintiffs who were not injured or prescribed the drug in California could not sue the company there.
cp-insurance-ireland: Personal jurisdiction is a right a defendant can lose by its own behavior. When a defendant ignores court orders to hand over facts about its ties to the state, the judge may treat those facts as proven and go ahead with the case.
cp-bremen: In this international admiralty contract, the agreed London forum was presumptively enforceable. Zapata had to show unreasonable or unjust enforcement, fraud or overreaching; merely preferring Houston was insufficient. The Court remanded to let Zapata attempt that showing, rather than finally deciding the contract dispute.
cp-zippo: This federal trial court distinguished passive websites from knowing, repeated online business with forum residents. Thousands of Pennsylvania subscriptions, claims arising from that business and reasonable litigation burdens supported jurisdiction here. Zippo’s influential framework is a trial-court approach, rather than a universal rule that website interactivity alone creates jurisdiction.
cp-shaffer: A state cannot reach a person just because they own some property there if the property has nothing to do with the dispute. Delaware could not hear a suit against company officers merely because their stock was treated as sitting in Delaware. Property claims face the same fairness test as everything else.
cp-burnham: If you are handed court papers while you are voluntarily in a state, even for a short visit, that state's courts can hear the case. A father served while visiting his kids in California could be sued there for divorce. The justices agreed on the result but not on why.
cp-mallory: Pennsylvania’s express registration-and-consent statute survived this due-process challenge: Pennsylvania Fire remained controlling. The Court did not decide the separate Commerce Clause challenge or treat every state’s registration law as consent. This is a consent route, distinct from the at-home test for jurisdiction based on business contacts.
cp-mullane: Notice must be reasonably calculated to reach interested people and let them object; due process does not guarantee actual receipt. Newspaper publication was inadequate for known present beneficiaries whose addresses the trustee had: they were owed at least ordinary mail. Publication could suffice for interests or whereabouts unascertainable with due diligence.
cp-szukhent: Parties to a contract can agree in advance to be sued in a certain place and can name someone to receive court papers for them. Because the named agent promptly passed the papers along, serving her was valid even though she never promised to do so.
cp-wyman: If a person is tricked into entering a state so they can be served, a resulting judgment is void. Wyman lured Newhouse into Florida by claiming her mother was dying and she was leaving the country for good, then had him served at the airport, so Newhouse could later defend against enforcement of that judgment in another state.
cp-sniadach: Wisconsin could not freeze earned wages under this procedure without notice and a prior opportunity to be heard. A later chance to recover the money did not cure the interim hardship. The Court reserved extraordinary situations needing special protection; it did not require a full merits trial before every provisional remedy.
cp-fuentes: A state cannot help a seller grab your household goods, such as a stove or a stereo, before you get a chance to tell your side. Getting the items back later does not fix the harm. Sellers must give notice and a hearing first, except in real emergencies.
cp-doehr: A person cannot lock up your house with a court attachment just by swearing out a claim against you if there is no hearing and no emergency. The court weighs your interest, the risk of mistakes and the claimant's need. Here the claimant had no stake in the house and had no reason to rush.
cp-lacks: Calling a legal requirement jurisdictional does not make a judgment void when it is broken. The divorce court had the basic power to hear divorces, and the residence rule only governed the claim itself. So the wife could not undo the final divorce on that ground.
cp-strawbridge: Under the 1789 diversity statute, each person sharing a joint interest had to be able to sue or be sued in federal court, so one shared state on each side defeated jurisdiction. Today's complete diversity rule grew from this reading.
cp-mas-perry: For state citizenship in diversity cases, a person must be a U.S. citizen domiciled in that state. Domicile combines residence with intent to remain and persists until a new one is acquired. Judy Mas’s temporary Louisiana graduate study did not change her Mississippi domicile; citizenship was assessed when suit began.
cp-afa: If a plaintiff claims over the federal dollar threshold in good faith, the court accepts that amount unless it is clear beyond doubt the claim is worth less. A judge should not dismiss on the spot but should let the plaintiff show why the claim is worth enough.
cp-mottley: A predicted federal defense does not create ordinary federal-question jurisdiction. The federal basis must appear in the plaintiff’s own properly pleaded claim. The Mottleys’ state contract claim failed that test; later cases explain the separate, narrow route for state claims necessarily raising substantial federal issues.
cp-american-well: A claim belongs to the body of law that creates it. A company sued under state law for hurting a business with false statements did not bring a patent case merely because patents might come up as part of the defense.
cp-shoshone: Congress allowing a certain kind of lawsuit does not by itself move that lawsuit into federal court. Adverse suits over mining claims go to any court that already has power. The suit must raise a real federal question or meet some other ordinary ground for federal jurisdiction.
cp-smith: A shareholder who sued to stop a bank from buying federally issued bonds raised a federal question, because the only reason the purchase would be unlawful was that the federal law behind the bonds was unconstitutional. A real federal issue at the core of the claim can be enough.
cp-grable: Some state-law claims can still go to federal court when a big, truly disputed federal question sits at the heart of the case. Here the dispute turned on whether the IRS gave proper notice of a tax seizure, which the federal government cares about, and such cases will be few.
cp-gunn: Being a case about a patent in the background is not enough for federal court. A client who sued his lawyer for malpractice over a patent argument raised a patent question, but its answer would not matter to the wider patent system, so the state court kept the case.
cp-gibbs: If your federal claim is real and a state claim comes out of the same events, the federal court can hear both in one case. Judges look at how the facts connect, not at labels, and they still choose whether to keep the state claim.
cp-aldinger: Under the statutes and precedent in force in 1976, the county was excluded from § 1983, and the Court would not append the state claim against it. That is a historical statutory holding: later developments changed municipal § 1983 liability, and § 1367 now expressly addresses supplemental claims involving additional parties.
cp-kroger: A plaintiff who sues one defendant and then finds that defendant has dragged in a third party cannot sue that third party directly in federal court if they share citizenship. Related facts do not fix the missing diversity.
cp-finley: In 1989, the FTCA’s grant over claims against the United States did not authorize related state claims against additional defendants. Finley required statutory authorization, beyond factual overlap. Congress subsequently enacted § 1367, which expressly includes additional-party claims subject to its exceptions; Finley’s restrictive approach is historical.
cp-exxon: In a diversity case, if one named plaintiff meets the dollar threshold, other plaintiffs or class members with smaller related claims can come along. The statute overrode the old rule that each plaintiff had to clear the threshold alone. The parties must still be completely diverse.
cp-shamrock: If you start a case in state court and the defendant answers with a counterclaim against you, you do not become a defendant who can remove it. Only the party that was sued can take the case to federal court.
cp-home-depot: A business pulled into someone else's lawsuit by a counterclaim cannot remove the case to federal court, even in a class action. Only the original defendant, the one sued in the plaintiff's own complaint, has that power.
cp-bechtel: A plaintiff cannot keep a case in state court by dressing up a federal claim in state-law words. Here Bright attacked federal tax withholding, so the claim was federal underneath and the case could be removed.
cp-wild-oats: Removing a case when the defendant is a citizen of the state where it was filed is a mistake you can lose by staying quiet. If the plaintiff does not object within thirty days, the judge cannot send the case back later on that ground.
cp-dart: When a defendant removes a case, it only has to say plausibly that more than the required amount is at stake. It does not have to attach proof unless the plaintiff disputes the number or the judge questions it.
cp-reasor: Arkansas judges were willing to hear a damages claim for harm to a crop on Missouri land. The court looked at why the old rule existed and refused to let the defendant escape any remedy just because the land was in another state.
cp-bates: In a federal debt-collection suit, you can file where the collection letter landed, because getting the letter is a key event behind the claim. The collector did not have to aim the letter at that place on purpose.
cp-livingston: In 1811, the court treated trespass to Louisiana land as a local action that could not proceed in Virginia merely because Jefferson was there. This is the historical local-action rule. Modern federal venue under § 1391 is determined without the local/transitory distinction, subject to other applicable law.
cp-hoffman: Under § 1404(a)’s 1960 wording, the destination had to be a district where the plaintiff could originally sue; the defendants’ later consent was insufficient. The current statute adds a separate alternative allowing transfer to a district to which all parties consent, while retaining convenience and justice requirements.
cp-piper: A court can send a case abroad as inconvenient even if the foreign country's law is less generous to the plaintiff. Foreign plaintiffs get less deference for choosing a US court, and Scotland counted as a fair alternative for the aircraft crash claims.
cp-atlantic-marine: A valid forum clause does not make otherwise proper venue improper. A clause choosing another federal district is enforced through transfer; one choosing a state or foreign court ordinarily through forum non conveniens. The plaintiff’s forum choice and private convenience arguments lose their usual weight, while public-interest factors remain.
cp-erie-decision: Federal courts deciding state-law rights ordinarily follow the governing state’s statutes and authoritative court decisions, rather than inventing general federal common law. Erie rejected the contrary Swift approach. It did not decide the railroad’s liability, or eliminate distinct federal rules where the Constitution, Congress or a recognized federal interest supplies them.
cp-swift: For a long time, federal courts ruled on general commercial questions by their own judgment and treated state court decisions only as respected opinions. That is the old approach Erie later threw out.
cp-taxicab: A company reincorporated in another state so it could sue in federal court, and the Court allowed it because the move was real and not a sham. Under the old Swift approach the federal court then applied its own view of general law.
cp-york: If a state would throw out your claim as too late, a federal court hearing the same state claim must do the same. Calling a rule procedural does not matter if ignoring it would change who wins.
cp-ragan: A federal case on a state claim can be too late even if you filed on time, when the state's own rule says the clock stops only on service. Filing under the federal rule did not give the claim a longer life than Kansas allowed.
cp-woods: If a state's courts would shut the door on you, you cannot walk through a federal courthouse in that state on the same state-law claim. Diversity jurisdiction gives you a different court, not a better chance to win.
cp-cohen-beneficial: A small shareholder suing on behalf of a company had to post security for expenses under state law, and the federal court had to follow that rule. The ruling is also why some orders can be appealed right away if they decide something separate that would be lost later.
cp-byrd: A strong federal interest in the judge-and-jury system outweighed South Carolina’s rule assigning this disputed statutory-employee issue to the judge. The state rule was not shown integral to the substantive right. Byrd received a chance to litigate the issue before a jury on remand; the Court did not decide his employee status.
cp-hanna-decision: First ask whether a Federal Rule covers the question. If it does, and it is valid, the federal court follows it. Only when no Rule applies do you ask the Erie questions about forum shopping and unfair treatment. Serving papers on a relative at home was fine under the Rule.
cp-sibbach: A federal rule is valid if it truly governs how courts run a case, even if it touches something personal like a physical exam. How important the interest is does not turn a procedural rule into a substantive one.
cp-walker: The federal rule on starting a case did not decide when the state's time limit stopped running. With no Federal Rule on that question, the federal court followed Oklahoma's rule that the clock stops on service, not on filing.
cp-stewart: When a valid federal statute answers the question, it beats a conflicting state policy in a diversity case. The transfer statute lets a judge weigh a forum-selection clause as one important factor, so a state rule ignoring the clause could not control.
cp-gasperini: A state's limit on how big a damages award can be applies in federal court too. The trial judge applies that standard first, and the appeals court only checks for abuse of discretion. The case involved lost photographs and a jury award of $450,000.
cp-shady-grove: Five Justices agreed that Rule 23 answered whether this suit could proceed as a class action and displaced New York’s restriction here. They divided over the Rules Enabling Act validity analysis. The Court restored the opportunity to seek certification; it did not certify the class or erase every state limit on class remedies.
cp-dice: A railroad worker's release of his rights under the federal injury law is judged by federal law, even in state court. If the railroad tricked him into signing, the release fails, and the state cannot take that fraud question away from the jury.
cp-clearfield: When the United States issues its own checks, federal law decides who bears the loss from a forged endorsement, not state law. Delay in giving notice only helps the defendant if the delay actually caused a loss.
cp-boyle: A military contractor can avoid state design-defect claims if the government approved precise specifications, the equipment matched them, and the contractor warned the government of dangers it alone knew about. Otherwise the state claim could raise military costs.
cp-gillispie: Under the old fact-pleading rules, you could not just say the defendants committed trespass, assault and confinement. Those are conclusions. You had to state the actual facts, and Gillispie was told she could amend.
cp-dioguardi: Under the Federal Rules, a self-drafted complaint over seized tonics did not have to state facts that make out a technical cause of action. A short statement showing the plaintiff may be entitled to relief was enough to go forward.
cp-conley: A complaint is fine if it gives fair notice of the claim and what it rests on, and it should not be thrown out unless the plaintiff could prove nothing that would entitle them to relief. Detailed facts were not required. Twombly later retired the no-set-of-facts wording.
cp-swierkiewicz: You do not have to plead the full proof framework for a job discrimination case in your complaint. Describing what happened, the dates, and the ages and nationalities of the people involved gave enough notice to proceed.
cp-twombly: A complaint needs enough facts to make your claim believable, not just labels. Showing that rival companies acted alike did not make an illegal agreement plausible, since each had its own reasons to act that way.
cp-iqbal: Courts ignore bare conclusions in a complaint and ask whether the remaining facts make the claim plausible. Senior officials are not liable for what their subordinates did just because of their rank. The complaint had to show the officials themselves acted with discriminatory purpose.
cp-kearns: If your whole case rests on a fraud story, you must plead who, what, when and where with particularity, even if fraud is not an element of the claim. Relabeling it as an unfair business practice does not avoid the stricter rule.
cp-tellabs: In securities fraud cases, the facts must point to intent to deceive at least as strongly as they point to an innocent explanation. A judge weighs the guilty and innocent stories together. A tie goes to the plaintiff.
cp-ziervogel: Under Missouri's rules, a harm like high blood pressure that was not pleaded and did not necessarily follow from the pleaded injuries cannot be proved at trial. It does not matter that the defendant already knew about it.
cp-garcia: A complaint can survive even if it is a bit messy, as long as the defendant can understand the claim. The court still ordered a clearer statement of the words said, and struck allegations about testimony at a Labor Department hearing because they were absolutely privileged.
cp-swanson: Plausibility does not mean a plaintiff has to prove the case in the complaint. It means telling a coherent story with enough specifics, here the discrimination alleged, who did it and the early-2009 transaction, to show what the claim is about.
cp-ingraham: The Fifth Circuit treated this Texas damages cap as an affirmative defense. Because the government first raised it after judgment, it lost the cap’s benefit in these cases. The decision explains that particular statute’s treatment under Rule 8(c), rather than classifying every damages limit automatically.
cp-kegerise: When you answer a complaint, you must respond to each part of every allegation, admitting what is true and denying the rest. You cannot dodge by calling a paragraph a legal conclusion. Here the fix was an amended answer, not an automatic admission.
cp-beeck: Aquaslide could amend its mistaken admission that it made the slide: the judge found no bad faith or unfair prejudice on this record. A separate jury then found it was not the manufacturer. Rule 15 favors amendment when justice requires, but withdrawal of an admission is not automatically allowed in every case.
cp-moore: A claim nobody pleaded counts as tried only if the other side knew it was being fought over and had a fair chance to respond. Evidence that merely fits a claim already in the case gives no such notice. Here custody stood but separate maintenance was reversed.
cp-krupski: When a plaintiff sued the wrong company and fixes it late, the question is what the company she meant to sue knew, not how careless she was. Costa Crociere should have known it was left out only because of a mix-up, so the Court reversed.
cp-surowitz: A shareholder who signs a verification in good faith, trusting careful work by advisers and lawyers, should not lose her suit because she cannot explain the complex deals herself. The rule exists to stop abusive suits, not to throw out honest ones.
cp-hadges: For sanctions requested by another party, Rule 11 requires a separate motion and the opportunity to correct or withdraw during its safe harbor, ordinarily twenty-one days. Those protections were skipped here, so the sanctions were reversed. Court-initiated sanctions follow a separate show-cause procedure and have no party-motion safe harbor.
cp-ellis-canning: Under Kansas’s real-party-in-interest statute, an insurer that paid the entire loss owned the whole subrogated claim. The insured could not sue in its own name for the insurer’s benefit, so the defense survived. The court did not decide partial-payment cases or make this Kansas rule a universal procedural requirement.
cp-harris-avery: A person who was falsely imprisoned and slandered in one episode can sue for both in a single petition, even though one harms the body and the other harms reputation. What ties them together is that the accusation, the taking of the horse and the detention were one event.
cp-heyward: If a defendant's counterclaim is closely tied to the same dispute, it must be raised in that suit, and a federal court can hear it without any separate basis for federal jurisdiction. Here claims over a private project were tied to a federal project's Miller Act suit.
cp-lasa: In a construction dispute where the supplier, subcontractor, prime contractor and architect all have claims against one another, those claims can be heard in one case if they are logically connected. If that gets messy, the judge can split the trials later.
cp-mosley: Plaintiffs can sue together if their claims grow out of related events and share some common question, even when their individual situations differ. An alleged general discriminatory policy was enough here, so the plaintiffs got to proceed jointly.
cp-bank-california: An absent person is not essential to a lawsuit just because the case touches them. If the court can write a decree limited to the defendants in front of it, the case can go on. Here each recipient owed a separate obligation, so the unserved beneficiaries did not have to be brought in.
cp-provident: Whether a case must be dismissed because someone cannot be joined is a practical judgment about fairness to everyone involved, not a label you attach first. Here the judgment was to be preserved if possible, with relief shaped to protect people who were not in the case.
cp-jeub: A defendant who might later be held liable can bring in the party who would owe it reimbursement now, without waiting until it has paid anything. The two disputes get decided together, but nobody has to pay until state law says the time has come.
cp-hancock: A stakeholder facing two groups that claim the same money can make them fight it out in one case, even if the stakeholder is a tenant who normally cannot question its landlord's title. Here both groups demanded the same lease royalties, so the lessees could bring everyone in.
cp-panamerican: This 1960 trial court allowed an insurer to interplead unliquidated claims competing for its limited policy fund, even while denying liability. Later, Tashire limited the injunction’s reach: interpleader can protect allocation of the fund without forcing every accident claim against insureds and other tortfeasors into that one case.
cp-tashire: Interpleader lets a stakeholder bring rival claimants into one federal case, and it only needs two claimants from different states. But the order stopping other suits can only protect the fund, here State Farm's $20,000. It cannot pull every suit against the drivers into the case.
cp-pimentel: If a foreign government with a serious claim to the disputed assets cannot be sued because of immunity, a court cannot go ahead without it by guessing it would lose. When its interests could be hurt, the case must be dismissed.
cp-smuck: The D.C. Circuit allowed the parents to intervene for an appeal, limited to decree provisions affecting their educational interests; the individual defendants lacked an appealable interest. The practical-interest intervention analysis was a three-judge plurality, rather than a majority explanation of every Rule 24 requirement.
cp-hansberry: A court cannot bind people to an earlier class judgment just because the earlier suit was labelled a class action. The people in that suit must truly have represented the interests of those being bound. Here their interests conflicted, so the earlier decree could not shut out the challenge.
cp-walmart: Putting many people in one class requires a shared question whose single answer would resolve a central issue for every member. Saying everyone was hurt under the same statute is not enough. These plaintiffs could not show a company-wide policy or a common way of using discretion, and individual backpay claims did not fit this kind of class.
cp-briseno: The Ninth Circuit rejected a separate requirement to prove an administratively easy way to identify every class member. Actual Rule 23 requirements still had to be met. The opinion discussed a different approach in the Third Circuit, so its rejection of this extra hurdle should not be presented as an unqualified nationwide rule.
cp-eisen: In a damages class action, every member you can find with reasonable effort must get individual notice. The named plaintiff normally pays for it, even if he cannot afford it. A judge cannot push 90 percent of the cost onto the defendants because the plaintiff looks likely to win.
cp-amchem: A settlement class has to meet the same class requirements as a litigated one, apart from worries about running a trial. A deal that looks fair does not make up for a class whose members had conflicting interests and too little in common. Here the class failed.
cp-ortiz: A class that forces everyone in, with no right to opt out, because there is not enough money to go around needs real proof that the fund is limited. Here the fund was not independently shown to be limited and conflicting claimants lacked separate representation, so the settlement could not be certified.
cp-standard-fire: Before certification, Knowles could not bind absent class members by promising that the whole class would seek less than $5 million. The court therefore had to ignore that nonbinding cap and aggregate their claims for CAFA jurisdiction. His promise could limit his own demand, but not theirs.
cp-transunion: Every class member seeking individual damages needs a concrete injury. Disseminated false terrorist-related credit alerts supported standing through harm analogous to defamation; undisclosed internal alerts did not on this record. A statutory violation or unmaterialized risk alone was insufficient for damages. The Court reserved the standing showing required at certification.
cp-shutts: A state can bind out-of-state class members on money claims if they get notice, a chance to be heard, a chance to opt out and fair representation. But the state cannot apply its own law to claims with little connection to it. Kansas could not apply its law to every transaction here.
cp-mussat: The Seventh Circuit held that a nationwide Rule 23 action under a federal statute needs personal jurisdiction over the defendant for the named representative, without a separate specific-jurisdiction showing for each absent member’s claim. It reversed the order striking the nationwide class allegations; it did not certify the class.
cp-cooper: Losing a class claim that the employer had a company-wide pattern of discrimination does not mean every worker's own claim fails, because individual decisions were never decided. The Baxter petitioners could still pursue their promotion claims but could not relitigate the pattern issue.
cp-concepcion: A state cannot insist that arbitration agreements allow class procedures, even if it calls the rule ordinary unconscionability law. That would change arbitration into something the parties did not agree to. Parties remain free to agree to class arbitration themselves.
cp-adickes: The side asking for summary judgment must first show there is nothing to try. If its own evidence leaves a gap, the motion fails even when the other side offers nothing. Here Kress did not rule out that a policeman was in the store and reached an understanding with an employee.
cp-celotex: A party moving for summary judgment need not prove the opponent's case false. It can point out that after enough time for discovery the opponent has no evidence on something it must prove at trial. The opponent must then show specific facts, here exposure to a Celotex product.
cp-anderson-liberty: A judge deciding summary judgment asks whether a reasonable jury could find for the other side under the burden of proof that will apply at trial. In this libel case that meant clear and convincing proof of actual malice. The judge does not weigh evidence or decide who is telling the truth.
cp-matsushita: When an alleged conspiracy makes little economic sense, ambiguous evidence is not enough to reach trial. Conduct that fits ordinary price competition as well as a conspiracy proves nothing alone. The plaintiffs needed evidence tending to rule out that the companies acted independently.
cp-dyer-macdougall: A plaintiff who must prove that someone said something cannot get to a jury just by hoping the jury will disbelieve witnesses who all deny it. With no admissible proof of his own, Dyer lost on summary judgment.
cp-scott: If a video plainly shows what happened, a court need not accept a version of events the recording flatly contradicts. Here the recording showed a dangerous chase, so the officer's intervention was reasonable. This does not let a court ignore a plaintiff's story whenever a defendant has video.
cp-tolan: Even when the issue is qualified immunity, a court at summary judgment must take the injured person's evidence as true and draw reasonable inferences in that person's favor. It cannot settle genuinely disputed facts against the plaintiff to make the officer's conduct look reasonable.
cp-arnstein: In the Second Circuit in 1946, summary judgment was off the table when there was even the slightest doubt about the facts, especially if the outcome depended on believing a witness the jury had not seen. Here Porter's denial of copying had to be tested before a jury.
cp-poller: In a complicated antitrust case where motive and intent matter and most of the proof sits with the defendants, a judge should be slow to end it on written affidavits. Acts that are lawful alone can still be part of an unlawful scheme, and that question deserves a trial.
cp-lexecon: When many cases are sent to one court for pretrial work, that court cannot keep them for trial by assigning them to itself. The statute requires each case to go back to the court where it started at or before the end of pretrial proceedings.
cp-hall: When one of several consolidated cases is finally decided, the loser can appeal right away without waiting for the rest. Consolidating cases puts them together for convenience but does not erase each case's separate identity.
cp-berk: In federal court, if a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure covers the question, it applies instead of a conflicting state rule. Delaware's affidavit-of-merit requirement gave way because Rule 8 already says what a plaintiff must show at the outset and does not demand evidence.
cp-cross: A judge should not end a case on summary judgment when the answer depends on motive and on whether the moving side's own witnesses can be believed. The other side may test that story by cross-examination at trial. Here the open question was the primary purpose of a trip.
lrs-s-brig-aurora: Congress can pass a law that switches back on when a future event happens, and let the President announce that the event occurred. The ship owner lost because he could not prove the cargo was American.
lrs-s-field: If Congress sets out the condition and what follows from it, the President only has to announce that the condition is met. That is fact-finding, not lawmaking. Also, a signed and filed bill stands even if the journals suggest it passed differently.
lrs-s-grimaud: Congress can write the broad rules and let an agency fill in the details, such as permits for grazing sheep in forest reserves. Breaking those rules can be a crime because Congress itself made it one and set the penalty.
lrs-s-hampton: Congress can let the President adjust tariff rates as long as it gives a clear goal to follow. Here the goal was to make up the difference in production costs between foreign and domestic goods, and that was enough guidance.
lrs-s-schechter: Congress cannot hand the President a blank check to write binding industry codes. A vague goal like fair competition gave no real limits, so the poultry code, and the convictions under it, fell.
lrs-s-yakus: Wartime price controls were allowed because Congress named the goal and the tool and drew lines a court could check. Congress could also force challenges into a special review court, so defendants could not attack the rule at their criminal trial.
lrs-s-amalgamated: A very broad grant of power can still be valid if the statute's purpose, setting and limits let people judge whether it is being followed. The court read fairness and review limits into the wage and price freeze power.
lrs-s-whitman: For national ambient air-quality standards, EPA could not weigh implementation costs: Congress specified health and welfare criteria. The statutory guidance satisfied the intelligible-principle test. An agency cannot cure an otherwise invalid delegation by promising self-restraint; the necessary standard must come from Congress.
lrs-s-gundy: A statute that seems to give an official huge freedom may be read narrowly. Four Justices read the sex offender law to give the Attorney General only transitional work, so the delegation passed. No five-Justice majority endorsed that reasoning.
lrs-s-buckley: Anyone who wields real power under federal law must be appointed the way the Constitution says. Congress cannot pick the people who enforce the election laws, so the Federal Election Commission could not use its enforcement powers as then constituted.
lrs-s-arthrex: Patent judges appointed as inferior officers could not issue these unreviewable final executive decisions. The remedy enabled the Senate-confirmed Director to review them. Arthrex was entitled to a decision from the Acting Director about whether to rehear its petition, rather than automatically receiving a new hearing or a new merits ruling.
lrs-s-freytag: A judge's helper who takes testimony and rules on evidence is an officer, not a mere employee. The Tax Court counts as a court of law, so its chief judge could appoint these special trial judges.
lrs-s-lucia: SEC administrative judges run trials, take testimony and decide cases, so they are officers and must be properly appointed. Lucia won a new hearing before a different, properly appointed judge.
lrs-s-shoemaker: When Congress gives an existing officer extra duties that fit the job, nobody needs to be nominated and confirmed all over again. Army engineers already holding their posts could sit on the park commission.
lrs-s-weiss: Military officers already appointed through the normal process did not need a second appointment to serve as military judges. The Constitution also did not give those judges a right to a fixed term of office.
lrs-s-edmond: These military appeals judges were inferior officers because Senate-confirmed superiors directed and supervised their work through the concrete controls shown. The Secretary could therefore appoint them. The Court did not claim that supervision is an exhaustive test resolving every possible principal-versus-inferior officer question.
lrs-s-myers: A postmaster was fired without the Senate's say-so, and the Court said the President alone may remove executive officers he appointed with Senate consent. Congress cannot make the firing depend on another Senate vote.
lrs-s-humphrey: In 1935, the Court upheld for-cause protection for FTC commissioners, characterizing the commission as quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial and distinguishing Myers’s postmaster. This is the historical exception. Trump v. Slaughter later overruled Humphrey’s Executor to the extent it permitted the FTC’s removal restriction, while reserving other institutions.
lrs-s-slaughter: The Court held that the FTC’s executive powers require presidential authority to remove its commissioners at will. It overruled Humphrey’s Executor to the extent that decision permitted the contrary FTC arrangement. Questions about the Federal Reserve and other entities or officials were expressly reserved.
lrs-s-wiener: In 1958, the Court inferred protection for this claims-adjudicating commission and rejected removal merely to install the President’s preferred member. It reserved removal for cause. That historical adjudicatory-body reasoning is distinct from later decisions about the FTC and other executive agencies; it is not blanket immunity for every adjudicator.
lrs-s-bowsher: Congress cannot keep the power to fire an official who carries out the laws. The Comptroller General answered to Congress, so he could not trigger the automatic spending cuts.
lrs-s-morrison: Congress may let a court appoint an independent counsel and may limit firing to good cause. That is fine as long as the President can still do his own constitutional job.
lrs-s-mistretta: Congress may ask a sentencing commission with judges on it to write the rules, if it gives clear goals. Putting that commission in the Judicial Branch did not upset the balance among the branches.
lrs-s-chadha: The House could not reverse Chadha’s deportation suspension through a one-House veto. That change to legal rights outside Congress was legislative and required passage by both chambers and presentment to the President, subject to the Constitution’s express exceptions. Presentment does not always require the President’s signature: a veto can be overridden.
lrs-k-holy-trinity: In 1892, the Court treated this church’s foreign-pastor contract as outside the labor statute despite its literal wording, relying on statutory purpose, context and consequences. The case illustrates that historical interpretive approach; it does not authorize judges to replace enacted text with their preferred policy whenever a result seems undesirable.
lrs-k-raila: The word transmission is read alongside its neighbors loss and miscarriage in the postal exception. So the exception covers mail that is damaged or delayed, and not a person hurt by a package carelessly left in the way.
lrs-k-dolan: A woman tripped over mail left on her porch, and the Court said the postal exception covers only mail that is lost, late, damaged or misdelivered. A trip on a carelessly placed package is not that, so her claim could go forward.
lrs-k-gayle: The phrase any court in the felon in possession law was read to mean American courts only. Looking at the rest of the statute and its history, the panel found no sign that Congress meant to count foreign convictions.
lrs-k-small: The word any does not stretch to every court in the world. Congress is assumed to be thinking of home, so a Japanese conviction did not count as the prior conviction that bars someone from owning a gun.
lrs-k-arlington-murphy: A law that lets winning parents recover attorney's fees does not quietly let them also recover expert witness fees. States taking federal money must be clearly told what they owe, and the text said nothing about experts.
lrs-o-noel-canning: The Clause covered sufficiently long recesses and vacancies already open when the recess began. Three days was too short; fewer than ten was presumptively too short. The Senate’s pro forma sessions counted because it said it was in session and retained the ability to conduct business, leaving these appointments invalid.
lrs-o-youngstown: During a steel strike the President seized the mills, and the Court said no. A President needs authority from Congress or the Constitution, and being Commander in Chief did not let him take over private factories.
lrs-o-tyson: An agency may set a health rule using imperfect and piled-up science and cautious assumptions. But if real risk remains and further protection is possible, it must explain with evidence why it did not go further.
lrs-o-londoner: Denver charged property owners for paving. Letting them mail in complaints was not enough. Before a bill for particular owners becomes final, they must get a real chance to be heard, with argument and proof.
lrs-o-bi-metallic: Due process did not require separate personal hearings before Denver’s general forty-percent assessment increase. Broad policy applied across the community, unlike Londoner’s individualized assessment. This constitutional distinction does not erase hearing or comment rights that a statute independently supplies.
lrs-o-jarkesy: If the government wants civil money penalties for something like securities fraud, which looks like old common-law fraud, the defendant can demand a jury in a regular federal court. The SEC cannot keep it in-house.
lrs-o-florida-east-coast: A statute saying an agency acts after hearing does not turn rulemaking into a trial. The railroads got to file written evidence and objections, and that was all the law required for this rule.
lrs-o-marathon-oil: The Ninth Circuit treated these fact-dependent permit adjudications as requiring formal APA procedures under the public-hearing language, despite the absence of the words “on the record.” It also required disclosure of data used against the applicants. The decision concerns adjudication, rather than imposing formal hearings on ordinary rulemaking.
lrs-o-perales: A doctor's written report can be used against a disability claimant even though it is hearsay and live witnesses disagree. The claimant had a right to call the doctor to the hearing and did not use it.
lrs-o-goldberg: Before welfare benefits are cut off, the recipient gets a hearing. That means timely notice, a chance to speak and bring evidence, and a way to question witnesses before a fair decisionmaker, because the money pays for food and shelter.
lrs-o-mathews: Due process weighs the private interest, the risk of error and value of added safeguards, and the government’s interests and burdens. For these Social Security disability procedures, written pretermination process plus later review sufficed without a prior evidentiary hearing. The Court did not approve termination without any opportunity to respond.
lrs-o-brock: A fired whistleblower can be reinstated temporarily before a full hearing. But the employer must first be told what the accusation is and the evidence behind it, and be allowed to respond. A trial-style hearing is not required.
lrs-o-roth: You can claim due process only if you lose a protected liberty or property interest. A professor on a one-year contract had no promise of renewal, so he had no property interest and was owed no reasons or hearing.
lrs-o-perry: A teacher without tenure can still win if he was let go for his speech, because the government cannot punish speech by withholding a benefit. He may also show that school practices gave him an unwritten tenure-like right.
lrs-o-arnett: Five Justices sustained these federal-employee discharge procedures: notice and a chance to respond before removal, with a fuller hearing afterward. Only three accepted the theory that statutory job protection came inseparably with its procedural limits. Loudermill later rejected that theory; “no prior trial-type hearing” did not mean no prior opportunity to respond.
lrs-o-loudermill: Your job protection comes from state law, but the Constitution decides how you can lose it. A tenured public employee must get notice of the charges, an explanation of the evidence and a chance to respond before being fired.
lrs-o-chenery-i: A court reviewing an agency order looks only at the reasons the agency actually gave. It cannot rescue the order by making a policy call the agency never made, even if the result could be defended on another ground.
lrs-o-chenery-ii: After being sent back, the SEC could reach the same result with a new and valid explanation. An agency may also choose to set policy case by case instead of by general rule, within its informed discretion.
lrs-o-wyman-gordon: The labor board announced a rule in one case without the notice-and-comment steps. The Court still enforced the later order against the company as a valid order in its own case, though the Justices disagreed about the earlier rule.
lrs-o-bell-aerospace: The labor board may decide new principles case by case rather than writing rules first. Managerial employees are outside the labor act altogether, so a company's buyers might be left without its protections.
lrs-o-national-petroleum: In 1973, the D.C. Circuit read the FTC Act’s §§ 5 and 6(g) to authorize substantive trade-regulation rules, enforced through the statutory complaint and hearing process. It decided rulemaking authority, not whether the octane rule itself was valid. The holding is tied to that statutory scheme, rather than every agency’s general rulemaking clause.
lrs-o-nova-scotia: In informal rulemaking, the public needed the scientific basis to comment meaningfully, and FDA had to answer major objections. The court rejected this rule as applied to non-vacuum-packed hot-smoked whitefish because relevant data were withheld and species-specific and feasibility objections went unanswered. It did not invalidate all fish-processing rules.
lrs-o-mock: At the preliminary-injunction stage, the Fifth Circuit found the challengers likely to win: the final firearm-brace rule was legislative, and its proposal did not give adequate warning of the final approach.
